newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Mediator calls for halt to fighting in E. Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Mediator calls for halt to fighting in E. Zaire.

text.p: Mohammed Sahnoun, an envoy dealing with the crisis in Central Africa, on Wednesday called for an immediate halt to escalating fighting in Eastern Zaire between government troops and ethnic Tutsi rebels.
Sahnoun, who represents both the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity, has been attending secretive talks in Johannesburg aimed at brokering a ceasefire.

His appeal was relayed by U.N. spokesman Juan Carlos Brandt in New York who said Sahnoun would report to Secretary-General Kofi Annan in Paris March 1 and come to U.N. headquarters to brief the Security Council.
He would then return to Nairobi, his main base, to attend a regional summit meeting on the Great Lakes region, which includes Rwanda, Burundi and other countries neighbouring Zaire.

"Ambassador Sahnoun is gravely concerned about the escalation of fighting in eastern Zaire, including the air bombings," the U.N. spokesman said, referring to raids by Zairean government planes against rebel-held areas.
The fighting was worsening the plight of the civilian population and of thousands of refugees, and impeding the delivery of humanitarian assistance, Brandt said.

"The large dispersion into inhospitable terrain of the inhabitants of eastern Zaire fleeing the fighting and the reported discovery of mass graves benefit no one and discredit all protagonists, no matter how legitimate their cause might be," he said.

Many of the refugees are Hutus, including former soldiers and ex-militia members, who fled Rwanda after the slaughter of more than 500,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994. They fear the Tutsi-led government now in power in Rwanda as well as the ethnic Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire.

"Ambassador Sahnoun calls, once again, on all the parties to abide by Security Council resolution 1097 (1997) and cease hostilities immediately," the U.N. spokesman said, citing a Feb. 18 resolution outlining a five-point peace plan for the region culminating in an international conference.

A halt to the fighting would enable the international community to "establish the facts and consider the practical modalities for the withdrawal of all foreign forces, including mercenaries," Brandt said.
It would also promote the establishment of a durable peace through dialogue, the electoral process and the proposed international conference, he added.
